doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Paul Gresham and sitting with Coltrane's quartet
summary: Record trading and friendship with Paul Gresham, who introduced him to McCoy Tyner and let him sit with Coltrane's band between sets for six nights.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: was, and you know Elvin Jones and McCoy, and Jim Garrison and stuff. And I was just doing some interviews of my dear friend who I spent a lot of time with whose name was Paul Gresham. He had a group called Birthright. And a little bit later in his group he had Ricky Ford.
The one that went to play with McCoy Tyner. Joe Ford or Ricky Ford.
I think Ricky Ford. I’m not sure.

Well whoever it was. And Paul looked just like McCoy Tyner. And as it turns out when he got on the road a little bit, we started trading records, as kids just out of high school. I just happened to meet him and he was with his cousin and two other black kids. We were cabbages. And we started, oh yeah, yeah, oh yeah, yeah. You collect records? I go yeah, I’ve got a lot of records, like maybe 15 hundred at the time you know, in high school. And he played a little bit, of piano, but saxophone. And so I remember the first time we met, on Delavan, on the east side of Delavan in the black community. And we went to his cousin’s house. And they told me to bring a couple of records, we were going to trade. So you’d get a couple of records you’d heard over and over again and you’d see what he’s got. So we hit it off real good. And he lived on Florida Street. So I would go to his house on Florida Street, and his mother was really fabulous. And then he’d come to my house. And he loved my mother. In fact he had her spaghetti sauce recipe, her coleslaw with pineapple recipe, and a few others. And so we loved each other’s mothers and we were there all the time. So he had got to meet McCoy in New York. So now this was the second time that Coltrane came in. So the first time I didn’t talk to Coltrane, you couldn’t talk to Coltrane, he was very serious and in bad shape. But this time he goes, “Charles, you’re going to love this, we’re going to sit with Trane in between every set, you and me.” He says, “I told him I got the hippest white boy in America. He knows more about jazz history than I do.” So there I was with Coltrane. Well he was having the teeth problems you know, with the sugar. He had a lot of sugar things. But we talked to McCoy. I was going you know, “Is that an e minor vamp” you know because Paul had shown me how to do a little bit of the “My Favorite Things” which I would play over and over, not well at all. And then Jimmy was nice to talk to. Elvin was just sort of aloof. But in between every set, for six nights, it was just remarkable. It was unbelievable. It was fabulous. And my non-interview with Thelonious Monk, we had a black kid who was a bad basketball player, Jimmy something, and he happened to be a worker at the Royal the hotel that was right next to the Royal Arms, it wasn’t called the Royal Arms, it was called the Stratford Arms.
